group.title: Science and research
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To repeat a study or test and get the same results.
examples: Other labs failed to {replicate} the surprising results.
wrong: They replicated the study by never running it again.

words.meaning: The checking of a study by other experts before it is published.
examples: The paper passed {peer review} and appeared in the journal last month.
wrong: Peer review means the author checks his own work alone in secret.

words.meaning: The people in a study who get no treatment, so results can be compared.
examples: The {control group} received a sugar pill instead of the drug.
wrong: Everyone in the control group got the new treatment first.

words.meaning: A factor in a study that can change and may affect the result.
examples: Temperature was the only {variable} we changed in the test.
wrong: A variable is something that can never change in any way.

words.meaning: A harmless pill with no medicine in it, used to compare results in a test.
examples: Half the patients were given a {placebo} without knowing it.
wrong: The placebo was the strongest medicine in the whole trial.

words.meaning: The fact of one thing directly making another thing happen.
examples: Two things rising together does not prove {causation}.
wrong: Causation means the two events had no link at all.

words.meaning: To put people or things into groups by chance, so the test is fair.
examples: We {randomized} patients into two groups by computer.
wrong: She randomized the groups by choosing her favorite people for each one.

words.meaning: To change facts or results dishonestly so they look different.
examples: The researcher was fired for {falsifying} his data.
wrong: She falsified the figures by reporting them exactly as they were.

words.meaning: To measure something and express it as a number or amount.
examples: It is hard to {quantify} the benefits of a good night’s sleep.
wrong: We quantified the damage by refusing to measure anything.

words.meaning: Describing a study that follows the same people over many years.
examples: A {longitudinal} study tracked the children until they turned forty.
wrong: The longitudinal study lasted only one afternoon.

words.meaning: A small amount or single example taken for scientific study.
examples: The lab tested a {specimen} of the river water.
wrong: A specimen is the whole collection, never a single sample.

words.meaning: The complete set of genes in a living thing.
examples: Scientists have mapped the entire {genome} of the rice plant.
wrong: The genome is the outer shell of a turtle.

words.meaning: A substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up.
examples: The metal acts as a {catalyst} and makes the reaction much faster.
wrong: Adding the catalyst stopped the reaction completely.

words.meaning: To make a substance by combining simpler chemicals.
examples: Chemists managed to {synthesize} the drug in the lab.
wrong: They synthesized the compound by breaking it into pieces.

words.meaning: The amount by which a measured result may differ from the true value.
examples: The poll has a {margin of error} of three percent.
wrong: A margin of error means the result is perfectly exact.

words.meaning: Too large to be explained by chance alone, according to math tests.
examples: The drop in cases was {statistically significant}.
wrong: The result was statistically significant, so it was probably just luck.

words.meaning: Very new and important, changing the way people think or work.
examples: Her {groundbreaking} research changed how we treat burns.
wrong: The groundbreaking study simply repeated old ideas.

words.meaning: A small first trial run to check a plan before the main research.
examples: We ran a {pilot study} with twenty people before the main trial.
wrong: The pilot study was the final and largest stage of the project.

words.meaning: A result that is very different from all the others in a set.
examples: One very high score was an {outlier} and was removed.
wrong: An outlier is a result that is exactly the same as the average.

words.meaning: To adjust a measuring tool so that it gives correct readings.
examples: Technicians {calibrate} the scales every morning.
wrong: He calibrated the thermometer so that it would show wrong numbers.

words.meaning: Something that happens or exists and can be observed or studied.
examples: The northern lights are a natural {phenomenon}.
wrong: A phenomenon is something nobody has ever seen or noticed.

words.meaning: Research done in the real world rather than in a lab or office.
examples: She spent a year doing {fieldwork} in the rainforest.
wrong: His fieldwork took place entirely at his office desk.

words.meaning: Describing a test where neither patients nor researchers know who gets the real treatment.
examples: In a {double-blind} trial, even the doctors don’t know who gets the drug.
wrong: In the double-blind study, every patient was told exactly what pill they took.

words.meaning: A thread-like part of a cell that carries genes.
examples: Humans have 46 {chromosomes} in most cells.
wrong: A chromosome is a large organ that pumps blood.

words.meaning: Able to be checked and shown to be true.
examples: Good science relies on {verifiable} facts.
wrong: The claim was verifiable, so nobody could ever check it.

words.meaning: To guess about something without having enough facts.
examples: It is too early to {speculate} about the cause of the illness.
wrong: She speculated about the result after reading the full, final report.

words.meaning: Based on facts from careful research rather than opinion.
examples: Doctors should follow {evidence-based} guidelines.
wrong: The evidence-based plan was built purely on rumors.

words.meaning: The number of people or things included in a study.
examples: With a {sample size} of just ten, the results are weak.
wrong: A large sample size means very few people took part.

words.meaning: Based on watching what happens rather than controlling it in a test.
examples: The {observational} study simply recorded how people ate.
wrong: In the observational study, scientists changed everyone’s diet on purpose.

words.meaning: Able to be done again with the same results.
examples: A result must be {reproducible} before others will trust it.
wrong: The result was reproducible, so nobody could ever get it again.

words.meaning: Able to be seen or noticed, and so studied.
examples: The drug had no {observable} effect on sleep.
wrong: The change was observable, so no one could see or detect it.

words.meaning: To suggest an explanation for something that has not been proved.
examples: Scientists {theorize} that the planet once had oceans.
wrong: He theorized about the cause only after it was fully proved.

words.meaning: Large enough or clear enough to be measured.
examples: The new diet led to a {measurable} drop in weight.
wrong: The change was measurable, so no tool could detect it.

words.meaning: A fixed limit or factor that controls how something is done.
examples: We set the {parameters} of the study before we began.
wrong: A parameter is a rule that nobody needs to follow.

words.meaning: A small test showing that an idea can really work.
examples: The small robot was a {proof of concept} for the larger design.
wrong: The proof of concept showed that the idea could never work at all.

words.meaning: To cut up a dead animal or plant to study its parts.
examples: Biology students {dissect} a frog in class.
wrong: They dissected the frog by keeping it whole and untouched.

words.meaning: So small that it can only be seen with a microscope.
examples: The water contained {microscopic} creatures.
wrong: The microscopic insect was as large as a cat.

words.meaning: To separate a substance or cause from others so it can be studied.
examples: Researchers {isolated} the gene responsible for the disease.
wrong: They isolated the virus by mixing it with everything else.

words.meaning: A change in the genes of a living thing.
examples: A small {mutation} made the virus spread faster.
wrong: A mutation is a gene that never changes in any way.

words.meaning: The process of testing ideas through observation and experiments.
examples: The {scientific method} starts with a question and a test.
wrong: The scientific method means believing an idea without testing it.
